title: Complementary Therapy Use and Parkinson’s Disease Symptom Severity and Progression: A Prospective Cohort Analysis Across Four Analytic Approaches
content: Background/Objectives: Parkinson’s disease (PD) progression is highly heterogeneous, and prognostic biomarkers guiding personalized management remain elusive. Complementary therapies are widely used by people with PD, their real-world associations with long-term symptom progression remain poorly characterized, and conclusions drawn from observational data depend on the analytic approach used. We examined baseline complementary therapy use in relation to symptom severity and progression using four complementary analytic approaches. Methods: Data came from the Modifiable Variables in Parkinsonism prospective cohort study (2013-present, n=2612 at baseline). Participants reported consistent use of 51 complementary therapies over the prior six months; the outcome was the Patient-Reported Outcomes in PD (PRO-PD) score. Four approaches were applied: (1) separate regression models for each therapy, (2) a multivariate model including the 24 therapies with ≥100 users, (3) unadjusted smoothed trajectories, and (4) linear mixed-effects models with a Time × therapy interaction. Adjusted models accounted for age, gender, income, and years since diagnosis. Results: Vitamin D (61.7%), vitamin B12 (39.7%), and fish oil (38.7%) were most frequently used. After accounting for concurrent use, low-dose lithium, fish oil, and oral glutathione were independently associated with lower baseline symptom severity. Baseline use of oral glutathione, coconut oil, estrogen, homocysteine-lowering B vitamins, multivitamin/mineral supplements, and inhaled marijuana predicted slower progression, whereas N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) and probiotics predicted faster progression. Associations frequently changed across analytic approaches, and several therapies reversed direction between cross-sectional and prognostic analyses. Only oral glutathione was associated with fewer symptoms or slower progression in every analysis. Conclusions: Findings about nutritional and lifestyle exposures depend strongly on the analytic approach, and cross-sectional associations were a poor guide to progression. Oral glutathione showed the most consistent favorable associations and warrants evaluation in interventional trials.
